During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints. Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning. To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone. Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment's joint configurations. We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data. To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector. In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18-32% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms. We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments. HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxi Jiang, Matthias Heyrman, Ren\'e Zurbr\"ugg, Marco Hutter, Christian Holz

item.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
item.description: arXiv:2610.25296v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.
item.dc:creator: Jize Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Xinyi Le, Cailian Chen, Xinping Guan, Dacheng Tao

item.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.25300v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.
item.dc:creator: Shi Feng, Qimin Zhong, Siwei Wang, Yifei Shen, Shang-Hua Teng, Hao Liao, Wei Chen

item.title: Shared-Private Cross-Modal Discrepancy Learning for Imbalanced Multi-Source Audio-Visual Deepfake Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.25301v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Audio-visual deepfake detectors are often trained under a single dataset or manipulation regime, but multi-source training collections may contain heterogeneous attacks and uneven source distributions. Training separate detectors for each source is inefficient, while a single shared detector may be biased toward dominant source-specific patterns. We study known-source imbalanced multi-source audio-visual deepfake detection using FakeAVCeleb and LAV-DF, where source identity is supplied during training and inference. To address this setting, we build on the Multi-Scale Cross-Modal Transformer Encoder (MSCT) and propose Pre-MSCT Shared-Private Feature Fusion. Our method routes \texttt{[CLS]}-augmented audio and visual tokens into a shared stream and source-specific private streams before the first MSCT block, while retaining its internal multi-scale self-attention (MSSA), differential cross-modal attention (DCA), and feed-forward operations. The shared stream models cross-source reusable evidence, while the private streams retain source-dependent residual variations. A domain-aware gated residual fusion module injects selected private evidence into the shared representation for the main fused prediction. Experiments under two controlled source-composition protocols show improved macro and worst-source AUC compared with the MRDF and MSCT baselines. These results support shared-private cross-modal discrepancy learning in the evaluated two-source setting with known source identity.
item.dc:creator: Qiwu Wen, Jahangir Alam

item.title: AdaFedXplain: Adaptive Federated Learning with Explainable AI for Ransomware Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.25318v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Attacks using ransomware have developed into complex multiphase campaigns that target vital infrastructure, resulting in annual damages of billions of dollars. Conventional detection techniques are ineffective against zero-day variations, and privacy issues are raised by centralized machine learning algorithms. Federated learning allows for cooperative model training without data sharing, however current FL approaches suffer from explainability issues, high communication cost, and non-IID data heterogeneity. In this study, we present AdaFedXplain, an explainable AI-based adaptive federated learning system for ransomware detection. Our approach includes progressive XGBoost complexity to avoid overfitting, a decaying learning rate schedule for stable convergence, and dynamic client grading based on ransomware prevalence and data sufficiency. Using 62,485 real-world ransomware samples from four OS-based non-IID clients, we compare AdaFedXplain against FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD. According to experimental data, AdaFedXplain outperforms all baselines with 99.59% detection accuracy and 99.64% F1-score while cutting energy usage by 75%, latency by 65%, and communication overhead by 75%. The ablation investigation demonstrates that every element enhances performance. Security analysts can use SHAP explainability to identify important PE header characteristics that influence detection decisions. Our system provides a collaborative ransomware detection solution that is efficient and interpretable, while reducing privacy risks through federated learnings data-local training paradigm.
item.dc:creator: Md. Emran Biswas, Md. Delowar Hossain, Mst. Tanbin Yasmin Tanny, Muhammad Aminur Rahaman, Md Al Amin, Tangina Sultana

item.title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
item.description: arXiv:2610.25323v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.
item.dc:creator: Tianyi Hu, Bhavyajeet Singh, Niket Tandon, Akhil Arora

item.title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
item.description: arXiv:2610.25341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.
item.dc:creator: Karthik Viswanathan, Plamen Dimitrov, Stefano Rocca, Sarayu Sirikonda

item.title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25352v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.
item.dc:creator: Jaehong Myung, Seunghun Oh, Unsang Park

item.title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
item.description: arXiv:2610.25356v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.
item.dc:creator: Ilia Badanin

item.title: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2610.25359v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Teacher takeover in on-policy distillation (OPD) can produce incorrect responses even when the student and teacher independently answer the same problem correctly, a failure we quantify using Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). To address it, we propose Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation (CD-OPD). CD-OPD structures the earlier context of teacher guidance through a teacher-generated dependency graph, curating the required problem conditions and preceding reasoning as node summaries alongside the unchanged guidance in a Contextual Digest before student continuation. We further develop online meta-reweighting, which compares Digest segment gradients with a task gradient from independent student responses to improve student-only performance, favoring updates predicted to reduce task loss. Across eight benchmarks, CD-OPD improves average accuracy by 1.32--7.05 percentage points over representative existing OPD methods. It also reduces CFR by 27.4\%--56.4\% relative to existing takeover-based OPD methods.
item.dc:creator: Mingyuan Li, Yucheng Li, Xiaxia Wang, Gong Cheng

item.title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
item.description: arXiv:2610.25362v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark. By releasing an evaluation benchmark, we provide a foundation for systematically studying and improving culturally aligned behavior in language models.
item.dc:creator: Junhong Liang, Daniil Orel, Saeed Almheiri, Bilal Elbouardi, Younes Samih, Abed Alhakim Freihat, Zhuohan Xie, Momina Ahsan, Muhammad Dehan Al Kautsar, Sarfraz Ahmad, Omar El Herraoui, Mohamed Anwar, Preslav Nakov, Fajri Koto

item.title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.25373v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.
item.dc:creator: Sen Gao, Yongan Li, Han Chen, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich, Shixuan Sun

item.title: MOSAIC: Multi-Objective Search for Allocating Inference Cache Across LLM Decoder Layers
item.description: arXiv:2610.25431v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score; its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search, and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48 points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). On both models, it reaches the score of uniform allocation with up to 4x less KV cache (75% smaller). Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10^40 x larger search space with 4x fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.
item.dc:creator: Sravanth Kodavanti, Manjunath Arveti

item.title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
item.description: arXiv:2610.25447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated "forget set" without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model $p_\theta$ to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor $p_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \Vert p_{\mathrm{anchor}})$. We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}} \Vert p_\theta)$ logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.
item.dc:creator: Tomer Garber, Tom Tirer

item.title: Reliability-Preserving Compression for Deployable Medical Image Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2610.25460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.
item.dc:creator: Sagar Kumar, Shailja Sharma, Tirthajit Baruah, Punit Rathore

item.title: DiaLong: Benchmarking Reminiscence in Long-Context Dialogues
item.description: arXiv:2610.25463v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Owen Bianchi, Samer Aslan, Ryunosuke Saito

item.title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.25481v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting of 3D anatomical changes is a critical generative vision challenge for modeling Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progression. While brain MRI forecasting from single-modality data has advanced, other key complementary multimodal biomarkers remain underutilized. In this work, we propose the Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Model (MC-LDM), a novel framework for patient-specific brain MRI synthesis. MC-LDM leverages multimodal biomarkers---MRI, tau-PET, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), and APOE4---during training, but relies only on baseline MRI, APOE4, and patient metadata at inference, reflecting realistic clinical availability. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) fine-tuned via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for data-efficient learning; (2) a multimodal conditioning that integrates molecular and clinical signals to model heterogeneous disease trajectories; and (3) auxiliary predictors estimating unobserved multimodal biomarkers from MRI features and patient covariates to condition the diffusion model, removing the need for these assessments at inference. Trained on 1,355 visits from 852 subjects in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), MC-LDM reduces average regional volumetric MAE by 18% over the second-best baseline on an independent test set of 664 visits. To our knowledge, MC-LDM represents the first diffusion-based framework to leverage multimodal priors for MRI forecasting. This conceptual advancement enables patient-specific trajectory generation that captures aspects of AD heterogeneity not observable from structural anatomy alone, bridging the gap between rich multimodal supervision and the strict constraints of routine clinical deployment. Code is available at: https://github.com/antonioscardace/MC-LDM.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Scardace, Silvia Ingala, Sebastiano Battiato, Daniele Rav\`i

item.title: PRIMA: Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter for Zero Shot Social Bodily Behavior Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2610.25482v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recognizing fine-grained bodily behaviors, such as self-grooming, postural shifts, and backchanneling, is a useful intermediate step for computational social signal analysis. But the behaviors that matter vary across social contexts, and retraining a model for each new taxonomy is expensive. Vision-language models (VLMs) can adapt to new categories through text prompts, yet they lack sensitivity to body structure and often confuse subtle postural distinctions. We propose PRIMA (Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter), a lightweight module that injects a body-structure prior into frozen VLMs using human pose as a training-time supervisory signal, requiring no pose input at inference. PRIMA separates a model-specific projection head from a shared core that encodes transferable body-configuration knowledge; adapting to a new VLM requires retraining only the head. We train PRIMA on a micro-action dataset and evaluate entirely through zero-shot prompting. The adapter improves recognition on its training domain, transfers to additional VLM backbones at different scales with the core frozen, and generalizes to two unseen target datasets from social psychology and daily activity recognition. In a supporting downstream study, the improved behavior predictions also yield higher correlations with human ratings of rapport and dominance in a collaboration context. Within the scope of the tested models and indoor datasets, the results indicate that pose-guided training can produce body-structure priors that generalize across unseen behavior vocabularies and can be partially reused across VLM backbones while preserving RGB-only inference.
item.dc:creator: Mingcong Ding, Babette B\"uhler, Tim F\"utterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Enkelejda Kasneci

item.title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
item.description: arXiv:2610.25511v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.
item.dc:creator: SM Mazharul Islam, Manfred Huber

item.title: When Interpretations Persist: Downstream Influence in Gaze-Aware Assistants
item.description: arXiv:2610.25512v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.
item.dc:creator: Mingcong Ding, Chenyan Zhang, Zhuojiang Cai, Dongyang Guo, Babette B\"uhler, Enkelejda Kasneci

item.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.25519v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.
item.dc:creator: Mobina Kashaniyan, Ali Jannesari

item.title: Modaliff: A Unified Token Diffusion Model for Any-to-Any Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.25533v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Any-to-any generation seeks a single model that translates flexibly among text, image, and audio, yet existing approaches either require fully aligned multimodal tuples or a shared representation that suppresses modality-specific structure. We introduce Modaliff, a novel token-based diffusion model that learns from widely available bimodal pairs while preserving each modality in its native latent sequence. Modaliff assembles conditions and targets into a unified token sequence, with per-token attributes to disambiguate token identities and role-based positional embedding to preserve each modality's internal structure across sequence layouts. This design enables a single denoiser to support diverse generation tasks without task-specific architectural changes or a shared cross-modal latent space. Beyond one-to-one generation, Modaliff supports multiple conditions either by combining single-condition predictions at inference or by lightweight finetuning on captions that jointly describe multiple inputs. Experiments across text, image, and audio show that Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and training data.
item.dc:creator: Duc Kieu, Kien Do, Minh Khoa Le, Tung Kieu, Dang Nguyen, Thin Nguyen

item.title: Residential Construction Image Dataset Using CSI Divisions for Deep Learning-based Object Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.25535v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate recognition of construction site elements is essential for the application of deep learning (DL) in the construction industry. Despite rapid advances in computer vision, the adoption of DL in construction has been limited by the lack of structured, publicly available datasets aligned with established industry standards. To address this gap, we introduce the Residential Construction Dataset Using CSI Divisions (ResCD-CSI) image dataset, a manually labeled image benchmark organized according to the divisional structure defined by the Construction Specifications Institute (CSI). The dataset comprises high-resolution images collected from active residential construction sites across the United States, capturing diverse building components, materials, and equipment under real-world conditions. In total, 16,365 objects spanning 14 major CSI divisions were precisely annotated using bounding boxes, ensuring consistency and reliability for object detection tasks. By aligning with the CSI divisional framework, ResCD-CSI establishes a standardized resource that bridges construction practice with computer vision research and supports the development of Artificial Intelligence-driven solutions for residential construction monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Fahad Iqbal, Shayan Mirzabeigi

item.title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
item.description: arXiv:2610.25575v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. In experimental materials disciplines such as perovskite photovoltaics, however, the most critical inquiries are inherently quantitative and aggregate measurements across dozens or hundreds of papers. Here, we present a quantitative question-answering benchmark where all 755 ground-truth answers are computed directly from 45,441 measured device records (40,889 human-curated records through 2021 and 4,552 records extracted from 2022-2026 literature). Benchmarking six retrieval architectures over 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU, standard passage retrieval tops out at 16-23% accuracy (compared to 1.6-6.5% zero-shot). In contrast, equipping the language model with read-only SQL execution over the structured device table elevates accuracy to 51.5% on historical and 50.8% on prospective literature -- a 33.01.8 percentage-point advantage over hybrid text retrieval. Aggregate queries spanning extrema, distributions, and filtered record counts prove virtually unsolvable via text retrieval alone, demonstrating that systematic table extraction is an operational prerequisite for literature-scale quantitative inquiry.
item.dc:creator: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou, Gaoxiang Yuan

item.title: When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
item.description: arXiv:2610.25603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As AI voice agents get deployed in high-volume contact centers, firms can route low-intent leads to AI and allocate high-intent leads to human workers. Drawing on sequential search theory, we posit that AI-induced task allocation reshapes work, enriching opportunities facing human workers but also raising their reservation value for continuing with the lead in hand, making them less willing to persist. We study the effects of an AI voice-agent deployment at a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage using more than a half million customer outreach records surrounding the rollout. Adopting a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we trace how worker behavior changes across the workday. Results show that the enrichment of human-facing opportunities concentrates early in the workday, raising the probability that a call is a high-intent lead by about 23 percentage points on the first three calls and fading to zero later. However, customer acquisition by human workers declines precisely where the enrichment is greatest, falling about 5 percentage points on the first three calls and flattening over the day. Consistent with the theorized reservation value mechanism, workers reallocate their earliest leads about 8 percentage points more often and persist less with them, shortening those calls by about 13%. A calibrated decomposition analysis further shows that the modest gain from improved lead ordering is outweighed by a much larger negative behavioral response. By reshaping the quality and within-workday distribution of opportunities, parallel AI deployment alters how workers pursue tasks, highlighting opportunity distribution as an important service operations state variable beyond workload and congestion.
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Fu, Shulong Luo, Narayan Ramasubbu, Peng Shen, Xincheng Wang, Yucheng Wang

item.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.25611v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.
item.dc:creator: Jesson Wang, Zhanhao Hu, Minghao Lin, Yuchen Wu, Aylin Caliskan, Mengyuan Li

item.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2610.25621v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.
item.dc:creator: William L. Tong, Aryo Lotfi, Emmanuel Abbe, Josh Susskind, Cengiz Pehlevan, Eran Malach

item.title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25626v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. We propose \textbf{MapSteal}, a student-independent framework for structured recursive knowledge acquisition. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal} {https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal}.
item.dc:creator: Zhengao Li, Chuxu Zhang, Yushun Dong

item.title: Selecting and Composing Agent Design Patterns: Industrial Case Evidence and Controlled Reference-System Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.25629v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent pattern catalogs describe architectural alternatives, but engineers also need evidence for selecting and composing them. We extend a cognitive-function--execution-topology framework with an evidence-driven selection procedure and explicit composition contracts. The study combines two industrial case accounts, a contributor's collaboration design, seven practitioner workshops, and executable fault-injection experiments. Three local reference systems use SQLite state, shared artifact files, and a file-backed map-publication surrogate. A 2 x 2 ablation separates function-specific contracts from execution controls across 36 scenario families, with ten input variants per family. Under equal family weighting, composition correctly completes or safely refuses 11 of 12 families in each system, compared with 2, 2, and 1 for the simple baselines. These are constructed challenge-suite results, not production success rates. Recovery without consumer-side verification increases false-success cases in the map surrogate. All composed systems still fail a boundary case in which trusted evidence is wrong. An audit of a frozen six-arm language-model pilot reproduces its scores but confirms an evaluator-dependent ranking reversal. The contribution connects industrial failure, pattern selection, executable treatment, external acceptance, and revision. Selection is demonstrated rather than evaluated against an alternative procedure; catalog admission rests on separate criteria. The results support bounded composition mechanisms, not a claim that the framework improves engineers' design decisions over an equally informative conventional method.
item.dc:creator: Jia Huang, Bingsheng Ru, Bo Liang, Yuke Xiong, Haiyan Fan, Joey Tianyi Zhou

item.title: ACorD: Adaptive Correspondence Discovery for Medical Image Registration
item.description: arXiv:2610.25638v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medical image registration is a fundamental task for aligning anatomical structures across images. Exhaustively searching for point-wise correspondences is prohibitively expensive in both computation and memory, particularly for high-resolution 3D medical images. Most recent learning-based methods directly predict correspondences in a coarse-to-fine manner, but often propagate intermediate estimates across scales without explicitly weighting correspondence evidence, which can allow coarse-scale errors to persist during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose ACorD, an adaptive correspondence discovery framework designed to mitigate error propagation with an attention-guided process. ACorD first predicts multiple potential correspondence candidates through Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (CCOP), which combines correlation maps as spatial matching priors with cross-scale features as global deformation context. Then, Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (MHDA) aggregates these candidate correspondences using attention, producing a learned, non-uniform weighting over competing matches rather than treating them equally. The multi-head design further captures complementary deformation patterns, ensuring both global alignment and local precision. By integrating adaptive offset prediction with selective, attention-based aggregation of correspondence evidence, ACorD enables accurate deformation refinement. Extensive experiments on four public medical registration benchmarks demonstrate that adaptive correspondence discovery within a multi-scale refinement framework improves registration robustness across diverse anatomical structures.
item.dc:creator: Arghavan Rezvani, Kun Han, Xiaohui Xie

item.title: Consistency Training Suppresses Cue Following Without Teaching Cue Selectivity
item.description: arXiv:2610.25650v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models often change answers because of a cue, a hint such as "I believe the answer is B" that gives no valid evidence. Consistency training (CT) trains a model to answer the same with and without the cue. Four CT methods apply this idea to output tokens (BCT), residual activations (ACT), attention patterns (AttCT) and sampled-answer rates (RMCT). Prior work suggests some learn different solutions. We train all four on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the same data. We test predictions written in advance and inspect the models with a known circuit that carries cues to the answer. All four make the trained cue less effective, and their fixes share three properties. First, correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones. Second, the fix is usually large for cues before the answer options, as in training, and much smaller after them. Llama RMCT depends least on position. Third, the circuit heads still carry most remaining cue-induced errors. Making BCT targets depend on the cue's correctness mostly weakens the fix. CT thus weakens the trained cue without teaching models when a cue is right. Evaluations with only wrong cues at the trained position miss the first two properties.
item.dc:creator: Prakhar Gupta, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Zhijing Jin

item.title: A "feature ODE" describing the learning behavior of shallow MLPs on simple functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.25652v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the gradient flow training dynamics of two-layer multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) on anisotropic Gaussian data. Even in this simple setting, solving the dynamics in full is notoriously difficult, so we try something different. We propose a "feature ODE" that might be intuitively expected to describe the learning dynamics of a shallow MLP. We find that MLPs trained to learn simple target functions (low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions) actually roughly follow the loss trajectories from this feature ODE. This agreement is a surprise because of the size of the simplification and the fact that it does not come from a rigorous chain of approximations. We discuss this surprise and speculate on its reasons and uses.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Turnbull, Berkan Ottlik, Jamie Simon

item.title: Beyond Leaderboards: A Method for Application-Specific Capability Profiling of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25659v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public leaderboards rank large language models (LLMs) in general, but an engineer has to choose a model for a specific application, architecture and cost. This paper presents a method for application-specific capability profiling of LLMs and its realization as a containerized testbed. The method treats each application as a unit of extension: an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration agent, a documentation-grounded chatbot or an enterprise-support automation agent runs in its own container behind a small contract, brings its own dataset, evaluator and owned attributes, and is onboarded together with its dashboards. Measurements accumulate in a versioned, sparse metamodel of every model. The method separates the model under test from judges and agents, freezes and hashes plans, refuses to compare values from different contexts, diagnoses the instrument before the system, and applies a null-agent check and a noise rule whose operating characteristics are quantified by simulation. In the evaluated automation conditions, model choices produced larger differences on selected observable outcomes than framework choices, although the experimental design does not establish a general causal ranking of these factors. The experiments also show that instruction tuning is deployment-specific and that system-reported success can exceed independently observed success: of 216 migration units checked against a real Oracle database, 108 were demonstrably correct. These measurements establish application-specific observations, not a universal model ranking.
item.dc:creator: Oleg Grynets, Vasyl Lyashkevych, Andrii Salyk, Dmytro Koziuberda, Dmytro Kostetskyi, Oleh Kaskun, Olena Pochernina, Alona Seletska, Oleksii Ilchuk, Viktoriia Tsymbal, Daryna Tukalo, Bohdan Saukh, Ivan Fedorchuk, Hryhorii Petrenko

item.title: Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
item.description: arXiv:2610.25678v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many scientific advances come from cross-pollination, carrying an idea from one field over to a problem in another. Yet retrieving papers across fields remains underexplored, with existing benchmarks confined to a narrow range of fields. We study cross-pollination retrieval, the problem of identifying transferable ideas across research fields, and introduce CPR-Dataset, a large-scale dataset constructed by mining cross-topic citations. Its evaluation split CPR-eval has 1,300 queries in 26 fields, and its training split CPR-train has 10,573 pairs. On CPR-eval, the best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26, whereas an LLM reranker reaches 0.81. Standard contrastive fine-tuning on CPR-train raises Recall@10 to as high as 0.70. The gain carries over to domains held out from training and to analogy and reasoning-intensive retrieval. On AnaloBench, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 33% over the untrained retriever, whereas training on three existing retrieval datasets lowers it. On BRIGHT, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 70%, more than twice the gain from those datasets. CPR-Dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/CPR-Dataset, and the code at https://github.com/SeokwonJung-Jay/Cross-Pollination-Retrieval.
item.dc:creator: Seokwon Jung, Yerang Kim, Yejin Kim, Alexander Rubinstein, Arnas Uselis, Sangwoo Park, Seong Joon Oh, Sangdoo Yun

item.title: MT-CC: Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Asymmetric Calibration Behavior in Class-Incremental Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.25689v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As deep neural networks are required to continuously adapt to evolving data, class-incremental learning (CIL) has become an active research area. However, most existing works primarily focus on improving accuracy while overlooking confidence calibration, which measures the trustworthiness of the model's predictions. Although temperature scaling (TS) is effective for static calibration, it has rarely been explored in continual settings where data distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Continual Calibration (MT-CC), a novel post-hoc calibration framework that addresses the asymmetric calibration behavior in CIL, where the rate of confidence changes does not align with the rate of accuracy degradation across tasks, leading to different levels of miscalibration. Our key contribution is to design multiple temperature parameters through a lightweight grouping network that separates samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals in CIL. Furthermore, a Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization is incorporated to promote intra-group consistency. Experiments demonstrate that MT-CC significantly improves calibration performance while maintaining accuracy, offering a principled framework for reliable continual learning.
item.dc:creator: Sungjun Yun, Yonghee Choi, Dong-Jun Han

item.title: Progress-Guided Preference Generation for Aligning Generative Control Policies
item.description: arXiv:2610.25692v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative policies have achieved strong performance in imitation learning tasks, but their success is often constrained by the limited availability of expert demonstrations. Although preference-based fine-tuning can leverage suboptimal rollouts to improve performance, existing approaches heavily rely on expensive human annotations. In this work, we introduce Progress-Guided Preference Generation (PGPG), an unsupervised preference alignment framework that eliminates the need for human-in-the-loop supervision. Our method leverages ordered coverage alignment to measure sequential progress relative to a small set of expert demonstrations, enabling the automatic extraction of pseudo-preference labels from autonomously collected rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce key enhancements to improve the reliability of these progress-guided preferences, enabling effective fine-tuning of pretrained generative policies without requiring manually designed reward functions. Extensive experiments across a suite of challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks demonstrate that PGPG outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning baselines. Moreover, our conceptually simple framework is broadly applicable across multiple classes of generative policies, demonstrating strong versatility when integrated with both diffusion and flow-matching policies.
item.dc:creator: Tung M. Luu, Tri Ton, Duc M. Nguyen, Xuan Thanh Nguyen, Nguyen Gia Binh, Quang Tan Nguyen, Vu Duong, Daniel Sonntag, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Vien Anh Ngo, Chang D. Yoo

item.title: Causal Humility: Governing the Authority of Fairness Claims Under Causal Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2610.25709v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI systems increasingly shape consequential decisions in employment, lending, healthcare, and public services, making fairness an important problem for auditing and governance. Fairness assessment often requires more than identifying disparities in outcomes; it also requires understanding how those disparities arise. Causal approaches to algorithmic fairness address this explanatory problem by representing pathways through which protected attributes and other factors may influence outcomes. Yet causal reasoning in sociotechnical systems remains uncertain: relevant confounders may be unobserved, causal directions contested, and conclusions sensitive to modeling assumptions and representational choices. We introduce causal humility as a governance framework for managing the relationship between epistemic uncertainty and causal authority. Drawing on causal fairness research, epistemology, political philosophy, and science and technology studies, causal humility has four requirements: making consequential assumptions and omissions visible; preserving contestability across defensible causal accounts; recognizing indeterminacy as a legitimate analytical outcome; and maintaining proportionality between evidentiary support and institutional authority or action. We operationalize these requirements through Causal Cards, a documentation artifact for recording the causal basis, assumptions, omissions, model dependence, and governance implications of fairness claims. Using the UCI Adult dataset as a worked epistemic demonstration, we show how different causal discovery procedures applied to the same observational data render fairness-relevant pathways visible, absent, or unresolved. Causal humility treats such disagreement as information about the limits of what can responsibly be claimed and the authority those claims should carry.
item.dc:creator: Khadija Zanna, Rodrigo Ferreira, Frederick L. Oswald, Akane Sano

item.title: Corrected Block Sparse Spectral Optimization: Exact Models, Finite Identification, and Local Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.25721v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The block generalized-power method pairs threshold-based support selection with inexpensive Stiefel updates, but the standard block formulation conflates two nonequivalent objectives and leaves inactive components, threshold ties, and post-selection refitting ill-specified. We rebuild the model from the primal. Eliminating each loading column from the normalized loading-ball problem gives a sum of soft-thresholded Euclidean norms (A-SUM); the squared-threshold objective in common use arises from a quadratic lift (A-SQ). We prove both identities, exhibit a two-component instance whose maximizers disagree, and specify explicit conventions for zero-response columns, ties, rank deficiency, and mask-before-refit. For A-SQ we separate the historical full-polar iteration from a safeguarded Riemannian ascent and prove, for the latter, whole-sequence convergence via a sufficient-ascent lemma, a relative-error lemma, and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, which applies because the soft-threshold objective and the Stiefel constraint are semi-algebraic. A strict threshold margin then forces finite identification of the support and sign pattern. The post-identification map is ordinary power iteration on the active covariance for a rank-one hard threshold, and the Frechet derivative of a coupled polar map for component-specific supports; a radius-based safe-screening rule follows from the same local analysis. Planted-spike experiments match the predicted identification time and local rates. On modern-AI panels (GPT-2 residual stream, ViT CLS stream, Pitprops) the thresholded block-sparse components match dense PCA on reconstruction and improve on it in monosemanticity and class specialisation. On three native-label scRNA datasets (Zheng17 FACS-sorted PBMCs, 68k donor-A with FACS-correlated labels, Tabula Muris) A-SQ beats dense PCA on cluster-recovery AMI by +0.023 to +0.044 at matched sparsity.
item.dc:creator: Omid Shams Solari

item.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
item.description: arXiv:2610.25725v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.
item.dc:creator: Haoqun Cao, Yurun Yuan, Tengyang Xie

item.title: No Matter Who You Are: Addressivity and Sycophancy in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25728v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. While post-training has been implicated as a cause, how it internally gives rise to sycophantic behavior remains insufficiently understood. Post-training transforms the model's output from text completion into utterances directed toward an addressee, thereby giving the output \textit{addressivity}. We hypothesize that the accompanying pressure to follow the addressee's instructions and align with their preferences links this addressivity to sycophancy. To test this, we use Sparse Autoencoders to extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and examine their relationship with sycophancy. Steering models with addressivity directions can amplify or suppress sycophancy, and this effect is observed only in post-trained models. Furthermore, comparing the internal mechanisms of both model types confirms that the association between addressivity and sycophancy is strengthened through post-training. Finally, through a controlled post-training experiment, we find that models are sycophantic not toward a specific addressee but toward any recognized addressee, suggesting that the presence of an addressee, rather than the addressee's identity, is what elicits sycophancy.
item.dc:creator: Seungjong Sun, Hyunmin Jun, Minsik Yoon, Eungu Lee, Choongwon Kang, Young Seok Woo, Jang Hyun Kim

item.title: A Calibrated Instrument for Detecting Disposition Drift in Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25735v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Before language models are released, they are tested for harmful traits such as willingness to carry out dangerous requests, deception, power seeking, and sycophancy. The safe behavior these tests certify may degrade as models are modified, by topical fine-tuning, new training data, or changes to settings such as the depth of their reasoning. Most work reports such drift as single summary rates scored by another AI model, without the error analysis needed to interpret them. We adapt a calibrated measurement methodology recently developed for assessing how inference optimizations affect the quality of model outputs. Applying it to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models, we first establish the instrument's precision, showing that shifts of a few percentage points can be reliably detected. We then induce drift deliberately by fine-tuning on correct and on subtly harmful medical and financial advice; harmful advice induces a far greater shift than correct advice. Most strikingly, a model that reasons before answering can conceal the shift almost entirely in its answers, even though a direct reading of its internal state shows that its disposition has moved. With reasoning switched off, the same model shifts steadily as the share of harmful advice in its training grows. These results demonstrate the importance of testing safety with reasoning turned both on and off.
item.dc:creator: Jerry Kaplan

item.title: Cognitively Decoupled Meta-Induction for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
item.description: arXiv:2610.25749v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) tackles downstream tasks conditioned on demonstrations. This paradigm relies heavily on neighbor-based matching between queries and demonstrations, limiting out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. For better generalization, rule-based inductive reasoning derives task-level regularities, which we term task-level inductive representations (TIR), before directly answering. However, existing methods lack generalizable inductive ability across diverse tasks. Inspired by meta-learning, we propose Cognitive-Decoupling meta-Induction (CoDI) for TIR-based inductive reasoning on general tasks. CoDI comprises a Cognitive-Decoupling Framework for query-blind TIR induction, and a Dual-Loop Meta-Inductive Learning method for cross-task inducer optimization. Empirically, CoDI achieves substantial performance gains on five ID and OOD benchmarks, and preserves OOD gains without explicit induction at inference. Code is available at https://github.com/Yuqian-Wang2277/codi-meta-induction.
item.dc:creator: Yuqian Wang, Yuanzheng Wang, Chaojun Xiao, Ke Xu, Bingxiang He, Jinghan Tan, Zijun Chen, Lu Chen, Yi-Xin Huo, Maosong Sun

item.title: Remember Less, Adapt Longer: Bounded-State In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Recurrent Summary Memory
item.description: arXiv:2610.25758v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) enables agents to adapt to new tasks without parameter updates, relying on memory to retain what they learn from experience. For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.
item.dc:creator: Jiawen Wang, Cheng Xue, Peng Zhang, Jochen Renz

item.title: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.25760v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little to rule-following, although it helps one model complete the task. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. Without reasoning, linear probes recover the state from the model's activations about as well as a text classifier recovers it from the transcript. However, decoding accuracy does not predict which interventions change the agent's actions. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step. The state that can be decoded without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.
item.dc:creator: Pedram Mouseli, Massieh Moayedi

item.title: AirMPA: A Meteorology-to-Pollution Adapter for Global Air Quality Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.25797v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate real-time forecasting of atmospheric pollutants is essential for reducing exposure risks and improving public health. Traditional numerical forecasting systems suffer from incomplete parameterizations, uncertain inputs, and high computational cost. Existing deep learning approaches improve efficiency, but often entangle meteorological and pollutant variables within unified forecasting frameworks, limiting flexibility and pollutant-specific representation learning. To address these challenges, we propose AirMPA, a decoupled autoregressive framework for meteorology-to-pollution forecasting. AirMPA predicts 13 atmospheric pollutants at 0.4{\deg} spatial resolution and 12-h temporal resolution using meteorological fields, emission priors, and historical pollutant concentrations. The model is built on an improved Swin-Transformer architecture with zonal release attention and dual-branch fusion, enabling more effective modeling of global transport continuity and heterogeneous pollutant dynamics. During training, AirMPA uses the fifth-generation atmospheric reanalysis from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ERA5) as meteorological forcing, while during inference it directly ingests forecast fields from external meteorological models, enabling stable autoregressive prediction up to 5 days ahead. Experiments show that AirMPA consistently outperforms Aurora and surpasses the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in approximately 90% of pollutant-lead-time evaluation cases over the 5-day forecast horizon, while outperforming CAMS on all variables beyond 48 h. These results demonstrate the potential of decoupled meteorology-to-pollution forecasting for global air quality prediction.
item.dc:creator: Yiheng Wang, Kai Zheng, Yuetan Lin, Fanglu Fan, Chenliang Tao, Guochao Chen, Hongliang Zhang, Hao Li

item.title: Optimizing Marketing Budgets for Social Influence: A Generalized Fractional Incentives Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.25823v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Marketing managers routinely allocate limited budgets across individuals in social networks whose responsiveness and influence vary substantially. We study the problem of Budgeted Generalized Fractional Influence Maximization (BGFIM), which captures the allocation of continuous levels of marketing spend across users in the presence of heterogeneous response and network spillovers. In this framework, adoption probabilities are governed by user-specific response functions that capture both baseline propensity and marginal responsiveness, while incentive costs vary across users. We propose a scalable solution approach based on a discrete greedy procedure with provable approximation guarantees, enabling tractable optimization under realistic budget constraints. Our formulation generalizes prior influence maximization models by allowing heterogeneous response and cost structures, providing a more flexible representation of targeted marketing interventions. Using experiments on multiple large-scale networks, we show that continuous allocation strategies can outperform standard heuristics and improve influence outcomes under heterogeneous conditions, and we illustrate how the framework can support profit-oriented decision making by identifying budget levels that balance marginal returns and costs. Overall, our results highlight the value of fine-grained budget allocation in networked marketing environments and offer a scalable approach for data-driven marketing resource allocation.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek K. Umrawal, Akhil Bhimaraju, Eliot W. Robson, Lav R. Varshney

item.title: Diffusion Language Models Change Speed Across Tasks and Languages
item.description: arXiv:2610.25835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion language models can write several tokens in one forward pass, and they decide during generation how many passes to spend. Two outputs of the same token length can therefore vary a lot in cost. To understand the underlying factors of this cost variation, we analyze two diffusion models across 10 tasks. We find that the number of forward passes per token depends heavily on the task. Text copied or lightly edited from the input is cheap, while open-ended writing is costly. In DiffusionGemma, generating a token for story writing requires more than three times as many forward passes as for grammar correction. Two output properties explain much of this gap: how much of it is new relative to the input, and how rare its words are within the task. The same holds within a single response when thinking is involved. The final answer is cheap when it repeats the model's reasoning trace and costly when it adds something new. In multilingual generation, we find that highly tokenized languages also require more passes per token, adding to the cost they already pay with more tokens. Finally, cost tracks correctness: on the same math problem, wrong answers take more passes per token than correct ones, and weighting candidate answers by decoding speed beats majority voting by up to 4.2 points at no extra cost. Taken together, our results show that diffusion's computational advantage depends on how much of the output is already determined, while its decoding effort offers a practical signal for making inference more efficient and reliable.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Fayyaz, Ali Modarressi, Daniel Israel, Lucas Bandarkar, Nanyun Peng
