In particular, VaDar is the first algorithm to solve challenging, long-horizon tasks in the RoboCasa suite, even when starting from a policy pretrained from behavior cloning with near-zero initial task success. Taken together, VaDar's successes suggest that subgoal information benefits actor-critic reinforcement learning by enhancing the efficacy of critic learning, whereas policy goal-conditioning is often unnecessary.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Saxena, Mehul Goel, Sreyas Venkataraman, Sarvesh Patil, Max Simchowitz

item.title: Reasoning-Aware Multicalibrated Reliability Predictors for Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.26645v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As people increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) for information, model providers need to communicate meaningful estimates of whether individual responses are correct or, more generally, reliable. In the context of hallucinations, existing work uses multicalibration to make such reliability predictions meaningful across application-relevant groups, such as prompt topics. Topic groups alone, however, can conceal systematic errors: within the same topic and confidence level, responses with different chain-of-thought (CoT) properties may exhibit opposing errors that cancel on average. In this work, we introduce reasoning-aware multicalibration, a framework that supplements application-relevant topic groups with groups derived from observable properties of CoT traces. We highlight that, theoretically, groupings based on CoT are "internally important", i.e., groupings for which the multicalibration guarantee is not societally crucial as it is for high-risk topics, but whose inclusion in the multicalibration procedure could easily and significantly improve predictive accuracy of the final reliability predictor. Empirically, we apply our framework to hallucination prediction and unsafe-response detection across a variety of benchmarks, and find that adding CoT groups to topic-based calibration reduces Brier score in both tasks. Interestingly, we find that multicalibrating with respect to CoT groups alone (without any topic information) already improves calibration across topics, suggesting that the predictor's errors depend on how the model reasoned, rather than what it was asked about in the prompt.
item.dc:creator: Ekaterina Fedorova, Alessandro Morosini, Chara Podimata

item.title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.26651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Maiwald, Roderick McNeill, Jaeyoung Lee, Matthew A. Clarke, Lennart Justen, Alejandro Acelas, Ivo Andrews, Giles Harper-Donnelly, Adam Moore, Sophie Rose, Oliver M. Crook, Felix Jackson

item.title: The Development of Sycophancy in Language Models: Tracing Vulnerabilities from Pretraining to Post-Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.26655v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models can change a committed answer to accommodate a user's opinion or pushback without new evidence. However, when this behaviour develops during training and what a released model inherits from earlier stages remain unclear. We follow 741 checkpoints of 30 open model lineages, from early pretraining to released models. We plant initial verdicts on moral scenarios and measure how far a model follows a user's stated opinion or abandons its verdict under pressure. In most lineages the behaviour is present before post-training, and its average strength changes in either direction, at different stages across lineages. A clearer pattern emerges at the level of individual questions. Beyond responses without pressure, pretraining behaviour predicts little of which questions a released model yields on. That pattern forms during post-training: on routes with supervised fine-tuning, the fine-tuning checkpoint predicts part of it and the preference-optimization checkpoint most of it. A sibling trained from the same base along another route predicts far less: for T\"ulu-3 8B, its own preference-stage checkpoint removes 85% of the remaining prediction error, a sibling 19%. Internal states add predictive information without changing this ranking. Similar average scores conceal different vulnerabilities, and training history matters for auditing a released model.
item.dc:creator: Haonan Huang, Chengkun Cai

item.title: Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: Mitigating Rubric Hacking through Latent Dimension Recovery and Balancing
item.description: arXiv:2610.26685v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rubric hacking limits both performance and training robustness in rubric-based reinforcement learning. By decomposing rubrics into sub-dimensions, we reveal the Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: as the total rubric score increases, certain sub-dimension scores systematically decrease, suggesting the model sacrifices specific quality aspects to optimize the aggregated objective. From the sub-dimension perspective, we observe two phenomena: (1) dimension imbalance, causing the policy to favor heavily covered dimensions; (2) dimension absence, leading to a systematic gap between rewards and true quality. To mitigate these issues, we propose Fair-Race Dimension Aggregation (FRDA), which has generations compete within each dimension separately to mitigate rubric imbalance, and Residual Semantic Dimension Completion (RSDC), which mines evaluation dimensions implicitly encoded in a holistic preference signal to complete rubric coverage. Experiments in chat, science, and medical domains indicate that FRDA mitigates rubric hacking with more stable improvements, while RSDC outperforms both single-reward training and naive multi-reward aggregation, yielding generally higher-quality responses.
item.dc:creator: Jianqiang Xia, Han Xu, Dianxi Shi

item.title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
item.description: arXiv:2610.26695v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.
item.dc:creator: Murat Guney Kemal, Robert Lieck

item.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.26747v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.
item.dc:creator: Saurav Jha, Qianli Liao, Robert Vernon, Sarath Chandar, Quentin Fournier

item.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
item.description: arXiv:2610.26754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.
item.dc:creator: Liana Patel, Rishabh Ranjan, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, Carlos Guestrin

item.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
item.description: arXiv:2610.26781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 16949 (2027) 395-411
item.dc:creator: Nardine Basta, Robin Carpentier, Benjamin Zi Hao Zhao, Dali Kaafar

item.title: Mise-en-Video: Fine-Grained 3D Control for Multi-Shot Video Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.26801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have enabled high-fidelity single-shot synthesis, yet practical storytelling creation requires multi-shot videos with both strong inter-shot consistency and fine-grained controllability. Existing multi-shot video generation approaches achieve strong consistency but still fall short in controllability. In this paper, we propose Mise-en-Video (MeV), a highly controllable multi-shot video generation framework that allows video creators to conduct staging the multi-shot in the 3D space and then generate the corresponding multi-shot video. To achieve this, our framework combines a hierarchical attention mechanism for multi-level narrative consistency with 3D-aware layout guidance for precise, per-shot spatial control. To support training and evaluation, we develop standardized annotation pipelines and construct a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot texts and oriented 3D bounding boxes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MeV consistently outperforms strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.
item.dc:creator: Yingshuang Zou, Xiaoyu Shi, Yawen Luo, Ziang Li, Qinghe Wang, Mengfei Li, Chengfeng Zhao, Xintao Wang, Pengfei Wan, Kun Gai, Yuan Liu

item.title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
item.description: arXiv:2610.26817v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.
item.dc:creator: Surya Ramachandiran, Yiming Li, Juan Mancilla-Caceres, Tao Ye, Jun Liu

item.title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages
item.description: arXiv:2610.26821v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.
item.dc:creator: Claytone Sikasote, Hussein Suleman, Jan Buys

item.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
item.description: arXiv:2610.26826v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.
item.dc:creator: Yuchi Wang, Rongyao Fang, Weihao Yu, Xilin Wei, Tiancheng Gu, Dingkang Yang, Hang Zhang, Dayiheng Liu, Hongsheng Li, Shuai Bai

item.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
item.description: arXiv:2610.26834v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.
item.dc:creator: Anamaria-Roberta Hartl, Levente Z\'olyomi, Michael List, G\"unter Klambauer, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter

item.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.26840v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.
item.dc:creator: Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tan Yu, Weijie Zhao

item.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
item.description: arXiv:2610.26847v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
item.dc:creator: Rui Shi, Xunjian Yin, Jiacheng Sang, Zichuan Liu, Shuyan Zhou

item.title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
item.description: arXiv:2610.26848v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.
item.dc:creator: Zekai Li, Jiayi Yu, Jinlu Zhang, Luyang Niu, Zekun Qi, Jun Zheng, Xuchuan Chen, Dairu Liu, Yintianrun Zhang, He Wang, Li Yi

item.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.26852v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Zehao Wang, Jianpeng Yao, Yuping Wang, Yiping Li, Jiaqi Li, Zhixu Li, Kanghoon Lee, Jinfeng Wang, Cong Liu, Zhaowei Tan, Jinkyoo Park, Jiachen Li

item.title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2610.26856v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.
item.dc:creator: Shiao Xie, Siyu Chen, Jianwei Lv, Xiandong Li, Yujin Wang

item.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
item.description: arXiv:2610.26860v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
item.dc:creator: Yu Zhou, Cheng-Fu Yang, Rui Sun, Di Wu, Sibo Peng, Mingyang Zhang, Zhen Yang, Ruiyi Zhang, Nanyun Peng, Zhe Gan, Kai-Wei Chang

item.title: Python Tool for Visualizing Variability of Pareto Fronts over Multiple Runs
item.description: arXiv:2305.08852v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hyperparameter optimization is crucial to achieving high performance in deep learning. On top of the performance, other criteria such as inference time or memory requirement often need to be optimized due to some practical reasons. This motivates research on multi-objective optimization (MOO). However, Pareto fronts of MOO methods are often shown without considering the variability caused by random seeds and this makes the performance stability evaluation difficult. Although there is a concept named \emph{empirical attainment surface} to enable the visualization with uncertainty over multiple runs, there is no major Python package for empirical attainment surface. We, therefore, develop a Python package for this purpose and describe the usage. The package is available at https://github.com/nabenabe0928/empirical-attainment-func. OptunaHub now provides our implementation at https://hub.optuna.org/visualization/plot_empirical_attainment_surface/.
item.dc:creator: Shuhei Watanabe

item.title: Generative to Agentic AI: Survey, Conceptualization, and Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2504.18875v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic AI builds upon Generative AI (GenAI). It constitutes the next major step in the evolution of AI with much stronger reasoning, learning, and interaction capabilities that enable more autonomous behavior to tackle complex, long-running tasks. Since the initial release of ChatGPT 3.5, Generative AI has seen widespread adoption, giving users firsthand experience. However, the distinction between Agentic AI and GenAI remains less well understood. To address this gap, our survey is structured in two parts. In the first part, we compare GenAI and Agentic AI using existing literature, discussing their key characteristics, how Agentic AI remedies limitations of GenAI, and the major steps in GenAI's evolution toward Agentic AI. We also distinguish between early Agentic AI aiming at reasoning and interacting and the increasingly emerging paradigm of self-improving Agentic AI that operates continuously and learns from its experiences by updating itself. This section is intended for a broad audience, including academics in both social sciences and engineering, as well as industry professionals. It provides the necessary insights to comprehend novel applications that are possible with Agentic AI but not with GenAI. In the second part, we deep dive into novel aspects of Agentic AI, including recent developments and practical concerns such as defining agents. Finally, we discuss several challenges that could serve as a future research agenda, while cautioning against risks that can emerge when exceeding human intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Schneider

item.title: Markovian Linguistic-Temporal Bridge: Unlocking the Potential of LLMs for Time Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2505.13175v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adapting pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) for time series forecasting primarily relies on token-level linguistic-temporal alignment, leading to the stacking of logically disjointed tokens as input. While empirically effective, these methods overlook a fundamental capability of LLMs: modeling linguistic logic and structure, rather than merely processing token features. To address this limitation, we propose the Markovian-Guided Structure-Aware Alignment (MGSAA). Our core contribution is a framework that transcends pointwise feature matching to achieve global structural isomorphism between the linguistic and temporal domains. Specifically, MGSAA distills latent evolutionary patterns of language within LLMs into a Markovian state transition graph, which is transferred as a structural prior to the time series domain. Under this prior, time series patches are decoded into latent states and then aligned via state-constrained cross-attention. Ultimately, MGSAA generates a token sequence topologically isomorphic to the LLM's inherent mental structure, reactivating its reasoning capabilities for forecasting. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that MGSAA achieves state-of-the-art performance, providing an innovative solution for cross-modal alignment in LLM for time series forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/sunzju/MGSAA.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 2026, pp. 22165-22180
item.dc:creator: Siming Sun, Kai Zhang, Xuejun Jiang, Wenchao Meng, Qinmin Yang

item.title: Empirical Analysis of Decoding Biases in Masked Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2508.13021v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have recently emerged as a promising non-autoregressive paradigm for sequence generation. However, their performance is highly sensitive to the choice of decoding strategy. In this work, we reveal that prevalent uncertainty-based decoding strategies induce two decoding biases in MDMs: rigid boundary bias and trivial token bias. These biases limit the model's reasoning ability and ultimately degrade generation quality. To address these challenges, we propose UNmasking Calibration for DecOding DEbiasing (Uncode), a decoding calibration framework that regularizes uncertainty-based decoding by incorporating two complementary priors to shape global decoding trajectories and promote content informativeness. Extensive experiments on three advanced MDMs across seven reasoning- and planning-intensive benchmarks demonstrate that Uncode consistently outperforms existing decoding strategies by more than 7%, while achieving performance comparable to autoregressive models of similar parameter scales. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Uncode.
item.dc:creator: Pengcheng Huang, Tianming Liu, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Shuo Wang, Tong Xiao, Zulong Chen, Maosong Sun

item.title: Distinguishing Performance From Competence in Evaluations of Humanlike Abstract Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2510.02125v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI reasoning models have exceeded human performance on the ARC-AGI-1 benchmark, but does that mean state-of-the-art models have the underlying competence (humanlike abstract reasoning) that the benchmark was designed to test? Here we investigate the abstraction abilities of AI models using the closely related but simpler ConceptARC benchmark. Our evaluations vary input modality (textual vs. visual), use of external Python tools, and reasoning effort. Beyond output accuracy, we evaluate the natural-language rules that models generate to explain their solutions, enabling us to assess whether models recognize the abstractions that ConceptARC was designed to elicit. We show that the best models' rules are frequently based on less abstract, more domain-specific concepts, capturing intended abstractions considerably less often than humans. In the visual modality, AI models' output accuracy drops sharply; however, our rule-level analysis reveals that a substantial share of their rules capture intended abstractions, even as the models struggle to apply these concepts to generate correct solutions. In short, we show that using performance (accuracy) alone can substantially overestimate AI competence in textual modalities while underestimating it in visual modalities, an illustration of the risk of mistaking performance for competence.
item.dc:creator: Claas Beger, Ryan Yi, Shuhao Fu, Kaleda Denton, Arseny Moskvichev, Sarah W. Tsai, Sivasankaran Rajamanickam, Melanie Mitchell

item.title: SELECT: Semantic Erasure Boundary Construction with Sibling Exclusive Counterfactuals
item.description: arXiv:2510.16342v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Concept erasure aims to suppress undesirable concepts in text-to-image diffusion models while preserving their generative capabilities. Existing methods often redirect target concepts toward predefined semantic anchors, but the influence of anchor selection on the scope of concept erasure remains insufficiently understood. Through causal tracing, we reveal that concepts with more dispersed causal effects tend to exhibit higher anchor sensitivity and lower erasure robustness. Controlled anchor interventions demonstrate that anchor selection affects target suppression and collateral damage to surrounding semantic concepts. These findings motivate us to formulate anchor selection as semantic erasure boundary construction. We propose SELECT (Selective Erasure via Local Exclusive Counterfactual Targets), a plug-and-play framework based on Sibling Exclusive Concepts (SECs), which are semantically close to the target but mutually exclusive in its defining attributes. SELECT jointly constructs a counterfactual redirection endpoint and a local retention set to balance target suppression and semantic preservation. SELECT filters candidates using contextual activation, and uses semantic coherence to identify context compatible redirection endpoints, while the remaining SECs serve as local preservation constraints. Experiments on object, celebrity, artist-style, and NSFW erasure show that SELECT strengthens target suppression over fixed general anchors and achieves suppression-preservation trade-offs, while reducing concept re-emergence and erosion.
item.dc:creator: Tong Zhang, Ru Zhang, Jianyi Liu, Zhen Yang

item.title: Reflection-Driven Self-Improving Language Model Agents for Adaptive RAN Slicing
item.description: arXiv:2603.10564v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adaptive control in AI-native networks remains challenging because tasks such as dynamic Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing require persistent trade-off decisions among spectrum efficiency, service quality, and reconfiguration stability. Conventional Reinforcement Learning (RL) compresses these competing objectives into handcrafted scalar rewards, requiring exhaustive tuning for a balanced trade-off. Language model (LM) agents provide a new path toward adaptive control because they can semantically represent complex preference relations, but prompt-based adaptation struggles to retain long-horizon interaction history due to finite context limits. We propose a Reflection-Driven Self-Improvement (ReDSI) framework that replaces scalar rewards with semantic feedback for continuous policy adaptation. This framework is built upon a Small Language Model (SLM) agent for fast decision-making, coupled with a bi-perspective reflection to transform interaction history into preference data, subsequently distilling long-horizon decision experience into the SLM parameters through preference-based fine-tuning. Evaluated on a dynamic RAN slicing task, our method achieves an optimal trade-off across multiple competing objectives, outperforming standard RL baselines and existing LM-based agents by demonstrating substantially greater sample efficiency. These results highlight a viable paradigm of self-improving LM agents for reward-free multi-objective continuous control in AI-native networks.
item.dc:creator: Yuanhao Li, Haozhe Wang, Geyong Min, Nektarios Georgalas, Wang Miao

item.title: From Language Models to Control Policies: Search, Selection, and Verification
item.description: arXiv:2603.20537v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Industrial process control demands policies that are interpretable and auditable, requirements that black-box neural policies struggle to meet. LLM-driven heuristic synthesis offers an alternative: a language model iteratively proposes and refines human-readable Python controllers using rich behavioral feedback from a simulator. We study this form of programmatic policy search on hot steel rolling, a physics-simulated, multi-pass control problem with competing objectives and hard equipment constraints, and address three questions that arise once the search is run at scale: how to split a fixed budget of LLM iterations between restarting and refining, how to deploy the resulting pool of heuristics, and how to verify it. Treating each search run as a randomized algorithm, we find across 52 independent runs that runs of moderate length match the hindsight-optimal budget allocation, and that Luby-style universal restarts reach this regime without problem-specific tuning. Because each heuristic is cheap to simulate, a small portfolio selected per job outperforms the best single heuristic, also under cross-validation and on out-of-distribution operating conditions on which the best heuristic stalls. Finally, an automated audit pipeline combining static analysis, Z3 proofs, and property-based testing proves key safety properties for all 174 synthesized heuristics; the stall, which neither the search reward nor these properties reveal, shows that the specifications must also cover progress.
item.dc:creator: Nima H. Siboni, Seyedreza Kiamousavi, Vahid Rostami, Emad Scharifi

item.title: AI Evaluation Should Require Standardized Item-Level Data Releases
item.description: arXiv:2604.03244v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This position paper argues that standardized item-level benchmark data should become the default infrastructure for AI evaluation. Current evaluations suffer from underspecified item selection, construct misalignment, and poor generalization; a disproportionate focus on aggregate model scores compounds these failures by keeping them undetected and unfixable. Without item-level evidence, validity claims cannot be assessed, resulting in inflated capability claims, misdirected research, and unwarranted trust in deployed systems. Our position is that valid evaluation requires empirical evidence from item-level benchmark data, including item content, test conditions, model responses, and item-level score statistics, and that the standardized release of such data should be treated as core AI evaluation infrastructure. Such releases also enable transparency, replicability, and auditability of evaluation results. To show that the norm is both feasible and consequential, we construct OpenEval, an item-level repository of 10.7M+ responses across 160K+ items from widely-used benchmarks, under a unified schema that the AI evaluation community can build upon. We demonstrate how item-level data can identify low-quality items, document construct misalignment, and recover validity evidence about benchmarks' internal structure. We address objections concerning contamination and coordination burden, and show that both are tractable relative to the costs of decisions made on inadequately validated evaluative claims.
item.dc:creator: Han Jiang, Susu Zhang, Dongyao Zhu, Yuzhuo Bai, Sang T. Truong, Xiaoyuan Yi, Sanmi Koyejo, Xing Xie, Ziang Xiao

item.title: Traceable Context-Enriched Knowledge Graph Generation with Induced Schemas
item.description: arXiv:2604.03496v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge graph generation typically relies either on predefined ontologies or on schema-free extraction. Ontology-driven pipelines enforce consistent typing but require costly schema design and maintenance, whereas schema-free methods often produce fragmented graphs with weak global organization, especially in long technical documents with dense, context-dependent information. We propose \textbf{TRACE-KG} (Text-dRiven schemA for Context-Enriched Knowledge Graphs), a framework that jointly constructs a context-enriched knowledge graph and an induced schema without assuming a predefined ontology. TRACE-KG captures conditional relations through structured qualifiers and organizes entities and relations using a data-driven schema that serves as a reusable semantic scaffold while preserving full traceability to the source evidence. Experiments show that TRACE-KG produces structurally coherent, traceable knowledge graphs and offers a practical alternative to both ontology-driven and schema-free construction pipelines. The code, experiments and prompts are available at \url{https://github.com/mosadddeq01/TRACE-KG}.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Sadeq Abolhasani, Yang Ba, Yixuan He, Rong Pan

item.title: Schema-Aware Planning and Hybrid Knowledge Toolset for Reliable Knowledge Graph Triple Verification
item.description: arXiv:2604.04190v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide a critical foundation for many AI systems, yet their automated construction inevitably introduces noisy triples that undermine data trustworthiness. Reliable KG auditing requires jointly examining internal structural constraints and open-world evidence, whereas existing methods often rely on a single evidence source or static, one-shot inference, limiting adaptive evidence acquisition and auditability. We propose SHARP (Schema-Hybrid Agent for Reliable Prediction), a training-free agent that reformulates triple verification as a dynamic process of strategic planning, active investigation, and evidential reasoning. SHARP uses retrieved historical verification trajectories and entity--relation schema information to construct a task-specific investigation plan. It then iteratively coordinates KG and textual tools to cross-validate structural and semantic evidence, producing a verification verdict with a transparent evidence chain. On independently sampled, balanced test sets constructed from FB15K-237 and Wikidata5M-Ind, SHARP achieves average accuracies of 87.1% and 93.6%, respectively. Controlled comparisons with standard RAG using the same evidence sources, together with ablation studies, further show that the gains arise not merely from external retrieval, but from the combined effects of schema-aware planning, memory augmentation, and iterative hybrid tool use.
item.dc:creator: Xinyan Ma, Xianhao Ou, Chang Li, Yexing Du, Zhihao Zhu, Shixin Jiang, Runxuan Liu, Dandan Tu, Ming Liu

item.title: Gypscie: A Cross-Platform AI Artifact Management System
item.description: arXiv:2604.10311v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, encompassing both traditional machine learning (ML) and more advanced approaches such as deep learning and large language models (LLMs), play a central role in modern applications. AI model lifecycle management involves the end-to-end process of managing these models, from data collection and preparation to model building, evaluation, deployment, and continuous monitoring. This process is inherently complex, as it requires the coordination of diverse services that manage AI artifacts such as datasets, dataflows, and models, all orchestrated to operate seamlessly. In this context, it is essential to isolate applications from the complexity of interacting with heterogeneous services, datasets, and AI platforms. In this paper, we introduce Gypscie, a cross-platform AI artifact management system. By providing a unified view of all AI artifacts, the Gypscie platform simplifies the development and deployment of AI applications. This unified view is realized through a knowledge graph that captures application semantics and a rule-based query language that supports reasoning over data and models. Model lifecycle activities are represented as high-level dataflows that can be scheduled across multiple platforms, such as servers, cloud platforms, or supercomputers. Finally, Gypscie records provenance information about the artifacts it produces, thereby enabling explainability. Our qualitative comparison with representative AI systems shows that Gypscie supports a broader range of functionalities across the AI artifact lifecycle. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that Gypscie can successfully optimize and schedule dataflows on AI platforms from an abstract specification.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Porto, Eduardo Ogasawara, Gabriela Moraes Botaro, Julia Neumann Bastos, Augusto Fonseca, Esther Pacitti, Patrick Valduriez

item.title: RADD: Retrieval-Anchored Discrete Diffusion for Multi-Modal Knowledge Graph Completion
item.description: arXiv:2604.25693v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-modal knowledge graph completion aims to infer missing links by integrating structural, visual, and textual information. However, global retrieval can leave fine-grained entity ambiguity unresolved, while shortlist-only prediction excludes answers missed by candidate selection. We propose Retrieval-Anchored Discrete Diffusion (RADD), a unified framework that turns retrieval uncertainty into a probabilistic reference for multimodal refinement. By anchoring discrete diffusion to the query-specific retrieval distribution, RADD learns how complementary multimodal evidence should revise entity preferences, coupling global retrieval with fine-grained disambiguation. Bidirectional learning unifies head and tail refinement, while coverage-aware inference adapts ranking corrections to candidate coverage without restricting predictions to the retrieved set. Experiments on three MMKGC benchmarks demonstrate RADD's effectiveness and consistent improvements over strong baselines and its matched retriever.
item.dc:creator: Guanglin Niu, Bo Li

item.title: Virtual Speech Therapist: A Clinician-in-the-Loop AI Agent for Speech Therapy Planning
item.description: arXiv:2605.01101v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a proof of concept of the Virtual Speech Therapist (VST), an intelligent multi-agent based system designed to support stuttering assessment and individualized therapy planning through artificial intelligence (AI) driven workflows. VST integrates deep learning (DL) based stuttering detection fSD with large language model (LLM) based agentic system to assist clinicians in developing evidence informed therapy plans. The VST system begins with the acquisition and feature extraction of given speech samples, followed by the detection of stuttering types. Building on these speech driven information S, VST initiates an agentic reasoning process in which specialized LLM agents autonomously generate, critique, and iteratively refine individualized therapy plans P. A dedicated CriticAgent {\pi}ca acts as a structured self-refinement mechanism, reviewing the generated therapy plans P and identifying areas for potential improvement in consistency, methodological soundness, and alignment with available evidence and professional guidelines. The resulting therapy plan P is presented then as a draft for clinician review. Clinician feedback can then be incorporated to produce a revised plan P, thereby maintaining a clinician-in-the-loop (CITL) paradigm. An initial evaluation, involving expert speech language pathologist (SLP) examines the clinical interpretability and feasibility of the generated therapy plans. Taken together, the results show the potential of VST to augment clinician-led therapy planning and provide a promising basis for future studies evaluating its integration into real world clinical settings. An interactive user interface for the proposed prototype is available online at: https://vocametrix.com/ai/stuttering-therapy-planning-agent, facilitating interactive stuttering assessment and stuttering therapy planning.
item.dc:creator: Shakeel Sheikh, Patrick Marmaroli, MD Sahidullah, Slim Ouni, Fabrice Hirsch, Goncalo Leal, Bjorn W Schuller

item.title: MOIRA: Policy Memory and Belief Revision for Language-Model Agents in Non-Stationary Pair Trading
item.description: arXiv:2605.01954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many sequential decision-making problems exhibit hierarchical structure, where high-level semantic choices constrain downstream actions and feedback is delayed and ambiguous. Learning in such settings is challenging due to credit assignment: performance degradation may arise from flawed abstractions, suboptimal execution, or their interaction. We study this challenge through pair trading, a domain that naturally combines long-horizon semantic reasoning for asset pair selection with short-horizon execution under partial observability. We formulate pair trading as a hierarchical reinforcement learning problem and propose a language-driven optimization framework in which both high-level and low-level policies are parameterized by large language models (LLMs) and optimized exclusively through prompt updates. Our approach leverages pretrained LLMs as hierarchical policies and uses trajectory- and episode-level textual feedback to adapt abstractions and execution without gradient-based fine-tuning. By explicitly separating abstraction selection from execution, the framework reduces non-stationarity across hierarchical levels and enables targeted adaptation under delayed feedback. Experiments on real-world market data show consistent improvements over traditional and LLM-based baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning.
item.dc:creator: Polydoros Giannouris, Yuechen Jiang, Lingfei Qian, Yuyan Wang, Xueqing Peng, Jimin Huang, Guojun Xiong, Sophia Ananiadou

item.title: Can LLM Agents Respond to Disasters? Benchmarking Heterogeneous Geospatial Reasoning in Emergency Operations
item.description: arXiv:2605.11633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Operational disaster response goes beyond damage assessment, requiring responders to integrate multi-sensor signals, reason over road networks, populations and key facilities, plan evacuations, and produce actionable reports. However, prior work largely isolates remote-sensing perception or evaluates generic tool use, leaving the end-to-end workflows of emergency operations underexplored. In this paper, we introduce Disaster Operational Response Agent benchmark (DORA), the first agentic benchmark for end-to-end disaster response: 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disaster events spanning 10 types, paired with expert-verified, replayable gold trajectories totaling 3,500 tool-call steps. Tasks span five dimensions that cover the operational disaster-response pipeline: disaster perception, spatial relational analysis, rescue and evacuation planning, temporal evolution reasoning, and multi-modal report synthesis. Agents compose calls from a 108-tool MCP library over heterogeneous geospatial data: optical, SAR, and multi-spectral imagery across single-, bi-, and multi-temporal sequences (0.015-10m GSD), complemented by elevation and social vector layers. We comprehensively evaluate 13 frontier LLMs on our benchmark, revealing three persistent challenges: 1) disaster-domain grounding exposes unique failure modes (damage-semantic grounding, sensor-modality mismatch, and disaster-pipeline composition); 2) agents are doubly bottlenecked by tool selection and argument grounding, where gold tool-order hints improve accuracy by only 1.08-4.40%, and alternative scaffolds yield at most a 3.24% gain; 3) compositional fragility scales with trajectory length, the agent-to-gold gap widening from 7% to 56% on long pipelines. DORA establishes a rigorous testbed for operationally reliable disaster-response agents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Junjue-Wang/DORA.
item.dc:creator: Junjue Wang, Weihao Xuan, Heli Qi, Pengyu Dai, Kunyi Liu, Hongruixuan Chen, Zhuo Zheng, Junshi Xia, Stefano Ermon, Naoto Yokoya

item.title: Beyond Cooperative Simulators: Generating Realistic User Personas for Robust Evaluation of LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2605.12894v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact with diverse users, including those who are unclear, impatient, or reluctant to share information. However, collecting real interaction data at scale remains expensive. The field has turned to LLM-based \emph{user simulators} as stand-ins, but these simulators inherit the behavior of their underlying models: cooperative and homogeneous. As a result, agents that appear strong in simulation often fail in real human interactions. To narrow this gap, we introduce Persona Policies (PPol), a plug-and-play control layer that induces realistic behavioral variation in user simulators while preserving original task goals. Rather than hand-crafting personas, we employ an evolutionary coding agent to discover persona generation programs optimized for human-likeness and behavioral coverage over real user conversations. The evolved program generates diverse, human-like personas for any task in the domain. Across 4 benchmarks--including $\tau^2$-bench Retail and Airline, ColBench, and WildChat--evolved PPol yield 28-72% absolute gains in fitness score over the baseline simulator. In blinded evaluations, annotators judged PPol users as 'human' 80.4% of the time, nearly 2x more than the baseline simulators. Training agents with PPol also improves real-world performance: our user study with live human-agent interactions showed that fine-tuning with our method boosted task success by +23% over default baselines. PPol thus offers a novel approach to strengthen simulator-based evaluation and training without changing underlying tasks.
item.dc:creator: Harshita Chopra, Kshitish Ghate, Aylin Caliskan, Tadayoshi Kohno, Chirag Shah, Natasha Jaques

item.title: Herculean: An Agentic Benchmark for Financial Intelligence
item.description: arXiv:2605.14355v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI agents advance, the central question is no longer whether they can solve isolated financial tasks, but whether their capabilities generalize across complete professional workflows. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this question because they evaluate either static competencies or agents within a single interaction structure. We introduce Herculean, a benchmark of end-to-end agentic financial intelligence that crosses agent architecture, backbone model, and four structurally distinct workflows: Trading, Hedging, Market Insights, and Auditing. Each workflow is implemented as an MCP skill that preserves its native state, actions, constraints, and outcome criteria, allowing intact agent systems to be evaluated under matched external conditions. Across 30 architecture--backbone configurations, we find that agent capability is not globally ordered. Workflow rankings are weakly aligned, changing the architecture frequently reverses performance under the same backbone, and each architecture concentrates failure in different forms of workflow control. These results establish that agent performance is an interaction between architecture and workflow demand, rather than an intrinsic property of the underlying model. Consequently, success on a single financial workflow provides little evidence of dependable, general financial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Xueqing Peng, Zhuohan Xie, Yupeng Cao, Haohang Li, Lingfei Qian, Yan Wang, Vincent Jim Zhang, Huan He, Xuguang Ai, Linhai Ma, Ruoyu Xiang, Yueru He, Yi Han, Shuyao Wang, Yuqing Guo, Mingyang Jiang, Yilun Zhao, Youzhong Dong, Xiaoyu Wang, Yankai Chen, Ye Yuan, Qiyuan Zhang, Fuyuan Lyu, Haolun Wu, Yonghan Yang, Zichen Zhao, Yuyang Dai, Fan Zhang, Rania Elbadry, Ayesha Gull, Muhammad Usman Safder, Nuo Chen, Fengbin Zhu, Tianshi Cai, Zimu Wang, Polydoros Giannouris, Yuechen Jiang, Zhiwei Liu, Mohsinul Kabir, Yuyan Wang, Yixiang Zheng, Yangyang Yu, Weijin Liu, Wenbo Cao, Anke Xu, Peng Lu, Jerry Huang, Mingquan Lin, Prayag Tiwari, Yijia Zhao, V\'ictor Guti\'errez-Basulto, Xiao-Yang Liu, Kaleb E Smith, Jiahuan Pei, Arman Cohan, Jimin Huang, Yuehua Tang, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Xi Chen, Xue Liu, Junichi Tsujii, Jian-Yun Nie, Sophia Ananiadou

item.title: Nexus : An Agentic Framework for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2605.14389v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models have emerged as highly capable reasoners, yet their performance in time series forecasting remains uneven across domains and levels of contextual grounding. This is primarily due to their suboptimal time series reasoning and numerical modeling capabilities. To tackle this, we introduce Nexus, a multimodal forecasting framework that bridges qualitative event reasoning with structural numerical modeling through principled statistical synthesis. Nexus follows three structured stages: (1) Temporal profiling and anchor generation, which distills the multimodal history into a timestamped causal-temporal profile and generates a forecast anchor (2) Dual contextual outlook generation, which produces decoupled macro and micro level forecast trajectories, and (3) Bayesian synthesis, which reconciles the forecasting anchor with both contextual forecast trajectories via closed-form Gaussian updating weighted by empirical error covariances. Evaluated across three diverse forecasting benchmarks constituting eight datasets spanning rich event contexts, abrupt shocks, and purely numerical series, Nexus consistently outperforms leading time-series foundation models and language model baselines, while providing interpretable causal reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Sarkar Snigdha Sarathi Das, Palash Goyal, Mihir Parmar, Nanyun Peng, Vishy Tirumalashetty, Chun-Liang Li, Rui Zhang, Jinsung Yoon, Tomas Pfister

item.title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Agent Reasoning via Signed Graph Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2605.19418v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) seek to improve reasoning by combining diverse perspectives from multiple agents. However, aggregation may overlook supportive, contradictory, and uncertain relations among their responses. As a result, useful dissent can be suppressed, allowing an incorrect majority to dominate the final decision. We introduce SIGMA, a novel Signed Graph-informed Multi-Agent reasoning framework that distinguishes support, contradiction, and uncertainty among responses from black-box LLM agents. SIGMA constructs a signed evidence graph, reassesses disputed relations, and forms reasoning communities while preserving distinct evidence. It then conducts bounded cross-examination between community representatives and adjudicates their evidence without treating community size as a proxy for correctness. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets, across multiple LLM backbones and diverse multi-agent configurations, demonstrate that SIGMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving notable gains in both accuracy and conflict-resilient performance.
item.dc:creator: Longgang He, Longzhu He, Shihao Peng, Daojing He, Chaozhuo Li

item.title: Benchmarking the Limits of In-Context Reinforcement Learning for Ad-Hoc Teamwork
item.description: arXiv:2605.24423v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In-Context Reinforcement Learning (ICRL) has enabled foundation agents to adapt instantaneously to novel tasks, yet its efficacy in Ad-Hoc Teamwork (AHT)-where coordination with unknown partners is required-remains unexplored. To rigorously evaluate this, we introduce a large-scale benchmark ICRL4AHT, built upon a high-throughput JAX implementation of Overcooked-V2. Our benchmark includes a large, diverse teammate suite spanning both RL and heuristic policies, enabling controlled train-test shifts, and provides a reproducible end-to-end pipeline for teammate generation, learning-history collection, dataset construction, and online multi-episode evaluation. We evaluate representative history-conditioned ICRL algorithms, including Algorithm Distillation (AD) and Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT), across millions of transitions. Results reveal notable limitations: contrary to their success in single-agent domains, these baselines fail to exhibit robust test-time adaptation in multi-agent settings. Specifically, these methods frequently underperform random baselines across both unseen teammate and unseen layout tracks, with no clear in-context improvement over long horizons. These findings highlight the challenges of strategic inference under partial observability within the OvercookedV2 AHT protocol, establishing our benchmark as a critical testbed for next-generation coordination algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Yuheng Jing, Kai Li, Ziwen Zhang, Jiajun Zhang, Zeyao Ma, Jiaxi Yang, Lei Zhang, Zhe Wu, Jinmin He, Junliang Xing, Jian Cheng

item.title: MUSE: Benchmarking Assembly Structure and Interface Geometry in Multi-Component Text-to-CAD Generation
item.description: arXiv:2605.28579v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently advanced text-driven 3D generation, yet generating CAD models that satisfy practical design requirements remains challenging. Existing benchmarks focus primarily on single-part CAD models and geometric similarity, providing limited assessment of assembly structure and interface geometry. To address this gap, we introduce MUSE, a Text-to-CAD benchmark for generating multi-component, editable boundary representation (B-Rep) assemblies. MUSE pairs practical design instances with structured \textit{Design Specifications} and evaluates generated outputs across four dimensions: code executability, geometric validity, structural and interface fidelity, and functional consistency. We further introduce Structure and Interface Evaluation (SIE), which combines reference Physical Assembly Graphs with direct B-Rep analysis to assess component correspondence, connectivity, interface types, and interface clearances. Experiments on proprietary and open-weight LLMs show that high execution success does not necessarily translate into correct assembly structure or interface geometry. Together, MUSE provides a benchmark and evaluation framework for studying multi-component Text-to-CAD generation beyond shape similarity. Our project website, including the leaderboard, dataset, and code, is available at \url{https://dong7313.github.io/muse-benchmark/}.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Dong, Zeng Chenbo, Zhi Li, Xiao-Ming Wu

item.title: VLA-Trace: Diagnosing Vision-Language-Action Models through Representation and Behavior Tracing
item.description: arXiv:2605.30117v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models transform multimodal knowledge into embodied control remains an open challenge. We present VLA-Trace, a progressive diagnostic framework that analyzes VLA models through a unified evidence chain from representation dynamics to causal control attribution and behavioral manifestation. It specifically combines cross-modal and checkpoint-drift centered kernel alignment (CKA) to trace representation evolution, attention knockout interventions to identify modality-specific control pathways, and rollout-level behavioral probes to examine grounding, shortcut dependence, and semantic following. Experiments on $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA reveal three key findings. First, the two models exhibit distinct modality-specific adaptation dynamics during VLA finetuning. Second, they rely on different multimodal routing strategies and layer-wise dependencies during action decoding. Third, although VLA policies excel at visually grounded trajectory generation, they remain limited in fine-grained semantic following. These findings highlight future directions for representation-preserving adaptation, causal VLA circuits, and compositional semantic control.
item.dc:creator: Haoyuan Shi, Xiancong Ren, Yingji Zhang, Qinfan Zhang, Jiayu Hu, Haozhe Shan, Han Dong, Jinpeng Lu, Yinda Chen, Yi Zhang, Yong Dai, Xiaozhu Ju

item.title: Distilling LLM Feedback for Lean Theorem Proving
item.description: arXiv:2605.30861v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-training for reasoning models typically combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, most commonly with GRPO. However, this algorithm suffers from sparse rewards, limited exploration, and mode collapse. Building upon recent works on self-distillation, we propose Feedback Distillation, a training method where the model is trained to match, at the token level, its own distribution conditioned on privileged feedback produced by a language model. Feedback Distillation offers token-level supervision and can inject external knowledge. Evaluating our method for Lean4 theorem-proving, we find that Feedback Distillation maintains greater diversity in generated trajectories than GRPO, yielding higher policy entropy and better pass@k scaling. The two methods are complementary: initializing GRPO from a Feedback Distillation checkpoint outperforms either method alone. All in all, our results suggest a promising avenue to improve post-training for complex reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Gaetan Narozniak, G\'erard Biau, R\'emi Munos, Ahmad Rammal, Pierre Marion

item.title: FAM-Bench: Benchmarking Condition-Aware Food-as-Medicine Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.31410v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Food AI can recognize dishes, ingredients, and nutrients. However, these abilities do not show whether a dish is suitable for a person with a specific health condition. They also do not test whether such decisions are grounded in the relevant food evidence. To address this gap, we introduce FAM-Bench, a Food-as-Medicine benchmark comprising 2,500 question instances constructed from 1,811 recipes across 13 diet-related health conditions. Gold annotations are derived from rule-based dietary guidance informed by published sources and nutrition professionals. The benchmark contains two complementary tasks: dish-level suitability assessment and comparative dish analysis. We evaluate open-weight and proprietary vision-language models under four prompting modes. Results reveal a substantial gap between suitability decisions and their supporting rationales, as well as limited performance on comparative ranking. These findings highlight persistent challenges in grounded, condition-aware food reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Mingyang Mao, Bhargav Rishi Medisetti, Utkarsh Grover, Tanvir Ibrahim, Wenyan Li, Tingting Zhang, Xiaomin Lin

item.title: Planning Takes More Than Token Prediction: Causal Plan for Benchmarking and Building Physically Grounded Embodied Reasoners
item.description: arXiv:2606.01810v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current benchmarks for embodied vision-language planning inadvertently favor linguistic next-token prediction over physically grounded next-state reasoning. This rewards models that mimic statistical language priors rather than track true causal dependencies, reducing complex physical planning to shallow sequence modeling. Hence, achieving genuine physical autonomy requires a fundamental shift from linguistically grounded token prediction toward physically grounded causal reasoning. To this end, we introduce Causal-Plan-Bench, a high-fidelity diagnostic suite spanning four causal dimensions, curated via multi-stage verification. To endow models with this capability, a four-stage annotation pipeline extracts structured interaction records from egocentric videos to construct Causal-Plan-1M, a dense million-scale corpus of explicit causal reasoning traces. Extensive evaluation reveals a striking gap: leading models struggle to demonstrate genuine physical agency -- even GPT-6-astra scores only 43.04. In contrast, our tailored training recipe enables Causal Planner to internalize the complex physical logic required for accurate next-state estimation. Built upon Qwen3-VL-8B, Causal Planner raises its backbone's score from 33.23 to 45.28, a 36.3% relative gain, and improves on three external benchmarks without benchmark-specific adaptation. We further observe an empirical Causal-Supervision Scaling Trend. Paired no-vision controls also reveal substantial visual dependence, while cross-judge comparisons and human scoring assess the reliability of automated evaluation. More importantly, we initiate the first effort to turn agents from superficial token predictors into physically grounded causal reasoners, bridging language modeling and world modeling.
item.dc:creator: Zheng Lu, Mingqi Gao, Qinlei Xie, Wanqi Zhong, Hanwen Cui, Zirui Song, Lijie Wang, Chong Luo, Bei Liu, Yiming Li

item.title: Evidence Acquisition and Stopping via Lattice Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2606.09433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sequential evidence acquisition requires deciding what to observe and when to stop from partial information. We introduce a complete-record view of policy supervision: each fully observed training instance defines a lattice of evidence subsets, with a stop/query decision at every node. For a modest number of evidence groups, this structure can be enumerated even when individual groups contain rich representations. Our method, Subset Lattice Distillation (SLD), scores subsets with a shared masked predictor, constructs multi-step decision targets by cost-sensitive backward planning, and distills them into an observed-history controller. Uniformly resampled masks train the student across the subset space, while combinatorial planning remains offline. Separating subset scores from acquisition prices allows the predictor to be reused when the policy is replanned for new costs. Our analysis identifies action-margin conditions under which privileged supervision preserves optimal online decisions. On retrospective influenza monitoring, SLD achieves higher phase F1 at lower acquisition cost than both the closest-cost adaptive baselines and the fixed full-evidence model. A geographic and seasonal holdout, price perturbations, and ablation studies provide further evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Yixuan Zhang, Yang Song, Jiayi Zhang, Jingqi Sun, Hao Wang, Samir Bhatt, Hengguan Huang

item.title: Frame-Conditioned Moral Computation in LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct: An Exploratory Mechanistic Interpretability Audit of Ethical Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2606.15507v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This exploratory observational study uses the Transluce platform to analyze the internal activity of Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct on 54 moral prompts in four batteries: dilemmas, policy, and meta-ethical questions (B1, 17); role-playing scenarios (B3, 6); and a structured trolley comparison varying the switching mechanism (B4, 15) or the people's identity attributes (B5, 16) with the other fixed. We record each surfaced neuron's normalized activation score, identity, and description and each cluster's title and size, classify them by an explicit description rule, and measure the prevalence and ranking of ethics-labeled neurons and clusters, the neurons' activation scores, and the model's verdicts and stated confidence. Prevalence is similar across batteries (about 5% of retained neuron rows) while ranking differs: in the trolley batteries the first ethics-labeled row has median position 3, versus 9 in B1 and B3, ethics labels are about four times as frequent among the ten highest-scoring rows as overall, and ethics-labeled rows have a higher mean activation score than other rows within prompts (47 of 54). We observe situational anchoring: prompt-setting vocabulary appears in prominent cluster titles and selected high-ranked neuron descriptions. B4-vs-B5 First Rank and Priority Ratio contrasts detect no difference. With one retained response per prompt, the coded outcomes for the 31 trolley responses are 19 recommending intervention, one recommending non-intervention, and 11 giving no definite recommendation. We distinguish prevalence, ranking, behavior, and causal contribution as audit targets, measure the first three, offer frame-conditioned moral computation as an organizing hypothesis with stated tests, and propose mechanistic alignment, causal responsibility of ethically relevant features under controlled frame variation, as a criterion admitting distributed implementations.
item.dc:creator: Ali Dasdan, Manan Shah, W. Russell Neuman, Chad Coleman, Kund Meghani, Safinah Ali

item.title: Scientific discovery as meta-optimization: a combinatorial optimization case study
item.description: arXiv:2606.26728v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery is fundamentally an optimization problem, defined by a vast ``state space'' of theories and experiments, and an evaluation criterion based on quality, novelty, and validity.
